questions.stem: X is continuous with density f. Which statement is always true?
options: f(x) is never larger than one
F jumps exactly where f peaks
questions.correctFeedback: Right — a single point holds no probability for a continuous variable; probability lives on stretches.
questions.incorrectFeedback: For a continuous X, every single point has probability 0. A density can exceed 1, and its height is never itself a probability.

questions.stem: A discrete X has F(2) = 0.7 and F(2−) = 0.4. Then P(X = 2) is…
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — mass at a point is the jump: F(2) − F(2−) = 0.3.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Mass at a point is the jump size: F(2) − F(2−) = 0.7 − 0.4 = 0.3.

questions.stem: X is uniform on (0, 1/4). What is its density on that stretch?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — height × width = 1 with width 1/4 forces height 4. Densities above 1 are fine.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The area must be 1 and the width is 1/4, so the height is 4. A density may exceed 1; only areas are probabilities.

questions.stem: From Lesson 4: for a discrete X, which pair can give different answers?
options: P(X ≤ a) and plain F(a) itself
questions.correctFeedback: Right — they differ by the jump at a, P(X = a). For a continuous X the jump is 0 and they agree.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The other pairs are identities. P(X < a) and P(X ≤ a) differ by the jump at a, which is P(X = a).

questions.stem: Which function could be a probability density?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — 2x is never negative on (0, 1) and its area is 1. The others have area 3, dip below 0, or have area 1/2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: 2x on (0, 1) has area 1 and is never negative. 3 has area 3; x − 1 is negative on (0, 1); 1/2 has area 1/2.
